name: Badger Ghost of Zulu
description: The Zulu people of Southern Africa possess a profound spiritual tradition where ancestors and animal spirits play central roles in daily life and cosmology. The honey badger or ratel (Mellivora capensis) is native to the Zulu territories of KwaZulu-Natal and is well known in African folklore for its extraordinary ferocity, intelligence, and fearlessness. In Zulu spiritual belief, the amadlozi or ancestral spirits communicate through animals, and certain animals are recognized as having special spiritual significance. The honey badger, known in Zulu as insizi or sometimes by other regional names, is respected as one of the most fearless creatures in the African bush. A badger ghost in Zulu tradition would be understood as a particularly powerful ancestral spirit manifesting in animal form, or as the spirit of the honey badger species itself. Its fearlessness in confronting predators far larger than itself makes it a symbol of courage and determination in Zulu culture. The honey badger's ability to defeat venomous snakes and raid beehives without harm marks it as a creature with special spiritual protection
source: Regional survey of Southern African Bantu oral traditions and folklore — Zulu, Xhosa, Shona, Sotho, and related peoples as documented by Bleek, Callaway, Junod, and ethnographic records from the 19th–20th centuries.

name: Badger Giant of Ute
description: The Ute people of the Great Basin and Rocky Mountain region possess a spiritual tradition deeply connected to the animals and landscapes of their high desert and mountain territory. The American badger (Taxidea taxus) is native to the Ute ancestral lands spanning what is now Colorado, Utah, and parts of New Mexico, where it inhabits the sagebrush plains and mountain meadows. In Ute cosmology, giants appear in traditional stories as beings that existed before the current human era, and animal giants represent the ultimate expression of each species' spiritual power. The Ute Badger Giant would be a figure of immense digging power and tenacity, capable of reshaping the landscape. Ute oral tradition includes stories of various giant beings that interacted with the animal people of the creation era. While Ute mythology more prominently features Coyote the trickster and other animal figures, the concept of a Badger Giant fits within the pattern of oversized animal spirits that taught humans important skills and established the natural order of the Great Basin environment
source: Indigenous North American oral traditions — spirits and beings documented across Native American and First Nations folklore as collected in standard ethnographic sources (Curtis, Boas, Mooney, Schoolcraft, collections of the Bureau of American Ethnology).

name: Badger Guardian of Ashanti
description: The Ashanti people of Ghana possess a highly developed spiritual tradition centered on the concept of the sunsum or soul that exists in all things, including animals, plants, and natural features. The Ashanti believe in various forest spirits and nature guardians known as mmoatia or sasabonsam that inhabit the wilderness, protecting sacred groves and natural resources. While the golden stool, the symbol of Ashanti nationhood, is associated with the sky spirit Nyame, and animals like the leopard, python, and crocodile hold particular royal significance, the badger is not a traditional Ashanti spirit animal. However, the African civet and other mustelids are known in West Africa. A Badger Guardian in Ashanti tradition would be understood as an abosom or minor deity associated with a specific natural area, perhaps a forest with rich soil or a mountainside with caves. The honey badger is known throughout sub-Saharan Africa for its fearlessness, and an Ashanti Badger Guardian would embody this quality as a protector of the boundaries between the village and the untamed wilderness, between civilization and the wild forces of nature
source: West African oral tradition, Akan/Ashanti folklore

name: Badger Nature-Spirit of Haida
description: The Haida people of Haida Gwaii and the surrounding Pacific Northwest Coast possess one of the world's most distinctive artistic and spiritual traditions, centered on the complex relationship between the human world and the natural world. The Haida nation is organized into two principal moieties, the Ravens and the Eagles, and within these, numerous clans possess crest animals that trace their lineage back to the time when animals could take human form. While the badger is not a traditional Haida crest animal, the concept of a nature-spirit would be understood within the Haida framework of supernatural beings that inhabit the forests, mountains, and waters of their archipelago. In Haida cosmology, everything in nature possesses a spirit or sg̱aaga, and certain places are inhabited by particularly powerful nature-spirits. The Badger Nature-Spirit would be one such being, associated with the forest floor, the rich soil of the temperate rainforest, and the underground burrows that connect the surface world to the realm beneath. Haida oral tradition includes many stories of animal people who taught humans important skills and established the social and ceremonial order that Haida people follow to this day
source: Pacific Northwest indigenous folklore, oral traditions

name: Badger Nature-Spirit of Passamaquoddy
description: The Passamaquoddy people of the Wabanaki Confederacy in the northeastern woodlands of North America possess a spiritual tradition that recognizes nature-spirits inhabiting every aspect of the natural world. The Passamaquoddy, whose ancestral territory covers what is now eastern Maine and western New Brunswick, have a deep relationship with the animals of the northern forest including bear, moose, beaver, and wolf. While the badger is not native to the dense coastal woodlands of Passamaquoddy territory, nature-spirits in Passamaquoddy tradition are not limited by geography but exist in the spiritual landscape accessible through dreams and ceremonies. A Badger Nature-Spirit would be understood as a being from a different ecosystem, bringing gifts of knowledge from the underground world. In Passamaquoddy cosmology, the world is divided between the visible and invisible realms, and nature-spirits serve as bridges between these realms. The concept of a nature-spirit aligns with the Passamaquoddy belief in Kiwahq, powerful beings that inhabit the wilderness and must be approached with proper respect and protocol
source: USA mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Badger Spirit of Aztec
description: The Aztec or Mexica people of central Mexico developed an elaborate spiritual cosmology featuring a vast pantheon of gods, goddesses, and nature spirits governing every aspect of life. The Aztec calendar or tonalpohualli assigns specific animals to each day, including the jaguar, eagle, coyote, snake, deer, rabbit, and others, though the badger does not appear as a day sign. However, the Aztec understanding of the spiritual world included countless nature spirits and animal essences that existed alongside the major deities. The American badger (Taxidea taxus) does not naturally occur in the Valley of Mexico, as its range extends only into northern Mexico, but the coati and other mustelids are present. A Badger Spirit in Aztec tradition would be considered a tlazolteotl or minor earth spirit associated with digging, underground knowledge, and the transformation of decay into fertility. The Aztecs had a complex classification of animal spirits including those that accompanied humans through life as tonal or companion spirits, and the badger could serve as such a spirit for those born under certain favorable astrological conditions
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

name: Badger Spirit of Creek
description: The Creek or Muscogee people of the Southeastern Woodlands possess a deep spiritual tradition centered on the balance between the human world and the natural world. The Muscogee Confederacy is organized around a ceremonial cycle that includes the Busk or Green Corn Ceremony, during which the renewal of the world is celebrated and the sacred fire is rekindled. In Creek cosmology, animal spirits are part of the web of relationships that maintain cosmic balance, and each animal carries specific teachings and powers. The badger is not among the primary animal clans of the Creek people, which include the Bear, Tiger, Bird, and Wind clans, but it would be recognized as a spirit with particular gifts. The American badger (Taxidea taxus) ranges into the southern regions of historical Creek territory, particularly in what is now Alabama and Mississippi. The Badger Spirit of Creek tradition would embody the qualities of determination, digging power, and the wisdom of the underground, teaching humans that some of the most important knowledge lies hidden beneath the surface of everyday experience and must be sought with patient effort
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Badger Spirit of Paiute
description: The Paiute people of the Great Basin region possess a rich oral tradition centered on animal spirits that inhabit the high desert and mountain landscapes of their ancestral territory. While Paiute mythology most prominently features Coyote as the primary trickster and creator figure, and Rabbit plays a significant role in their storytelling, the American badger (Taxidea taxus) is native to the Great Basin and would have been a familiar presence in Paiute daily life. In Paiute cosmology, animal spirits serve as teachers and guides, each offering specific gifts to the human community. The badger, known for its extraordinary digging ability and fierce temperament, represents the qualities of persistence, protection, and connection to the underground world where powerful spirits dwell. Paiute elders would teach that the badger spirit demonstrates how to access hidden resources, both physical and spiritual, that lie beneath the surface of the visible world. The badger's ability to survive in the harsh Great Basin environment makes it a symbol of adaptability and resilience
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Badger Spirit of Passamaquoddy
description: The Passamaquoddy people of the Wabanaki Confederacy in northeastern North America have a spiritual tradition where animal spirits serve as clan totems and personal guides. While the badger is not native to the Passamaquoddy's coastal and woodland territories in what is now Maine and New Brunswick, the Passamaquoddy worldview holds that animal spirits are not strictly limited by geography but exist in the spiritual landscape accessible through dreams, visions, and ceremonies. In Passamaquoddy cosmology, the spirits of animals from distant lands bring unique gifts and perspectives that enrich the community's understanding of the natural world. A Badger Spirit in this context would be understood as a being that teaches about the power of persistence and the importance of digging beneath the surface of things to find hidden truths. The Passamaquoddy people, whose name means Those of the Dawn, maintain a deep connection to all animal beings as relatives with their own wisdom and teachings, and the badger spirit, though not a traditional clan animal, would be welcomed as a teacher of the virtues of determination, grounding, and the courage to face challenges from a position of low strength rather than high power
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Badger Spirit of Pomo
description: The Pomo people of northern California possess a complex spiritual tradition centered on the Kuksu religion, a ceremonial system involving masked dances and the veneration of spirits called Kuksu or Guksu who represent supernatural beings. While Pomo cosmology prominently features Coyote, Bear, and various bird spirits, the American badger inhabits the coastal ranges and valley regions of traditional Pomo territory. In Pomo understanding, all animals possess spiritual power and can serve as guides and teachers. The badger, known in Pomo territories for its digging prowess and fierce temperament, represents the qualities of tenacity, earth connection, and the ability to access hidden resources. The Pomo people have a deep knowledge of the plants and animals of their region, and the badger's role in aerating soil and exposing edible roots would not go unnoticed. In Pomo spirituality, animal spirits are often associated with specific dances and ceremonies, and the Badger Spirit would be called upon during rituals related to earth, healing, and the gathering of underground resources like medicinal roots and materials for basket making
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Badger Trickster of Aymara
description: The Aymara people of the Andean highlands in Bolivia, Peru, and Chile possess a rich tradition of trickster figures that challenge social norms and teach important lessons through their mischievous behavior. The primary trickster in Aymara folklore is the fox, who appears in countless stories as a clever but often unsuccessful schemer. The badger is not native to the high Andean plateau where the Aymara people live, as the region's extreme altitude and cold climate are inhospitable to these lowland creatures. The concept of a Badger Trickster in Aymara tradition would represent an outsider figure, a stranger from a different ecosystem bringing unfamiliar wisdom and methods. In Andean cosmology, the world is divided into three realms: the hanan pacha or upper world, the kay pacha or middle world, and the ukhu pacha or inner world. A badger trickster, with its digging abilities and underground dwelling, would be particularly associated with the ukhu pacha, the inner world of ancestors, seeds, and hidden forces. This trickster would teach that wisdom can be found in unexpected places and that the stranger's perspective often reveals truths that locals cannot see
source: Bolivia mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Badger Trickster of Cree
description: The Cree people, whose traditional territory spans across much of Canada from the Rocky Mountains to the Atlantic coast, have a rich tradition of trickster figures, most notably Wisakedjak or Whiskey Jack, who appears in countless stories as a transformer and culture hero. The rabbit or hare also plays a significant trickster role in some Cree traditions, as does Coyote in more western territories. The badger, while present in the southern portions of Cree territory, is not traditionally a primary trickster figure in documented Cree mythology. However, in Cree cosmology, all animals possess spiritual significance and some individuals might receive a badger as their personal spirit guide or totem. A Badger Trickster in Cree tradition would be an inventive addition to the existing pantheon of trickster figures, bringing the particular qualities of badger nature into the framework of Cree storytelling. This trickster would use its digging abilities and fierce temperament in ways that both cause trouble and reveal important truths about the world. The Cree oral tradition is living and adaptive, incorporating new characters and stories that address contemporary concerns while maintaining connection to traditional values and teachings
source: Canada mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Badger Ghost of Blackfoot
description: The Blackfoot Confederacy, comprising the Siksika, Kainai, and Piikani nations, possesses a profound spiritual tradition where animals appear as messengers, guardians, and spirit beings in dreams and visions. While the Blackfoot people traditionally venerate the buffalo as their primary animal relative and also hold the eagle, wolf, and bear in high regard, the badger appears as a lesser-known but significant spirit figure. In Blackfoot cosmology, ghosts are not necessarily malevolent but are spirits that remain connected to the physical world for various purposes. The American badger (Taxidea taxus) inhabits the Northern Plains and is known to the Blackfoot as a creature of remarkable ferocity despite its small size. In Blackfoot tradition, animal ghosts are sometimes encountered by vision seekers during their solitary quests on the prairie. A badger ghost appearing in such visions would deliver messages about persistence, protection, and the importance of knowing when to fight and when to burrow away from conflict. The badger ghost represents the enduring spirit of the land itself, a guardian of buried knowledge and ancestral memory In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.
source: Blackfoot spiritual tradition; documented in Plains indigenous records.

name: Badger Giant of Blackfoot
description: The Blackfoot Confederacy of the Northern Plains possesses a rich tradition of giants and oversized beings that inhabited the world in ancient times. In Blackfoot cosmology, the Niitsitapi or Real People share the world with various powerful beings, some of enormous size. The concept of a Badger Giant fits within this tradition of powerful, oversized animal beings that possessed spiritual significance and often interacted with humans during the mythical age before the world took its current form. The American badger is known to the Blackfoot people as a creature of remarkable ferocity that could serve as a model for a giant spirit being. In Blackfoot oral tradition, giant animal beings were often the original forms of animals that later shrank to their current size as the world changed. These giants possessed supernatural powers and knowledge that they sometimes shared with humans who treated them with proper respect. The Badger Giant would be one such being, representing the ultimate expression of badger qualities including underground power, tenacity, and fierce protection of home and family In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.
source: Blackfoot spiritual tradition; documented in Plains indigenous records.

name: Badger Giant of Tlingit
description: The Tlingit people of the Pacific Northwest Coast possess one of the most complex and visually stunning artistic and spiritual traditions in North America. Their social structure is organized around moieties and clans, each with crest animals that hold deep spiritual significance. The principal crest animals of the Tlingit include the Raven, Eagle, Wolf, Bear, and Killer Whale, while the badger is not traditionally a Tlingit crest animal. However, the concept of a Badger Giant fits within the broader Tlingit tradition of powerful animal spirits that existed before the current world order was established. The Tlingit believe in various giants and larger-than-life beings that inhabited the world during the time of the animal people, when creatures could speak and take human form. A Badger Giant would be understood as one of these ancient animal people, possessing immense power and wisdom. While the badger does not feature prominently in Tlingit folklore documented by ethnographers, the tradition of giant beings including the most powerful that are known as Nah or giant spirits creates a framework for understanding what such a being would represent in Tlingit cosmology In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.
source: Tlingit folklore; documented in Northwest Coast indigenous ethnographic records.

source: Tlingit folklore; documented in Northwest Coast indigenous ethnographic records.

name: Bahri Spirits (Moroccan Sea Jinn)
description: Bahri spirits (from Arabic 'bahr' meaning sea) are a class of water-dwelling jinn in Moroccan folklore that inhabit the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea along the Moroccan coast. They are considered the most dangerous of all jinn in Moroccan belief, as they are completely alien to human nature and do not share the terrestrial realm with humans. They appear as half-fish, half-human creatures with green eyes, scaled skin, and webbed hands and feet. Bahri spirits are blamed for shipwrecks, drownings, and disappearing fishermen. They enchant sailors with beautiful songs (like the Greek Sirens) or drag swimmers underwater. They are most active during storms and at sunset. Some traditions say they are led by a king named Sakhr or reside under the sea in crystal palaces. They are unique among jinn for being unable to cross fresh water
source: Moroccan oral tradition, Maghrebi Islamic folklore

name: Bai-Ulgan
description: Bai-Ulgan, also known as Bai Ülgen or simply Ülgen, is a prominent deity in the traditional shamanic religion of the Mongolian and Turkic peoples of Central Asia. He is the chief of the good deities, a creator god who dwells in the upper world, associated with the sky, light, and cosmic order. In Mongolian shamanism, the universe is divided into three realms: the upper world of the deities, the middle world of humans, and the lower world of dark spirits. Bai-Ulgan presides over the upper world, sitting on a golden throne at the summit of a cosmic mountain, where he judges human actions and maintains the balance of the universe. He is particularly associated with hunting, mountains, and wildlife, serving as the protector of animals and the enforcer of ethical hunting practices. Bai-Ulgan is not merely a passive deity but an active force in human affairs, rewarding those who respect nature and punishing those who take more than they need. His worship involves offerings, prayers, and the guidance of shamans who can ascend to his realm through ritual journeys to seek his blessing for hunting expeditions or to petition for the well-being of their communities
source: Altai Turkic religion — Bai Ulgan supreme creator deity.

name: Bai Ze
description: Bai Ze is a legendary chimeric creature from Chinese mythology, first recorded during the Tang Dynasty, known for its extraordinary wisdom and supernatural perception. According to ancient Chinese texts, Bai Ze appeared to the Yellow Emperor, Huangdi, during his reign around 2600 BCE, revealing the secrets of all the supernatural beings in the world. This encounter resulted in the creation of an encyclopedia of spirits and demons, a text that became foundational for Chinese demonology and exorcism practices. Bai Ze is said to possess complete knowledge of every creature, spirit, and demon that exists, including their names, appearances, and methods for warding them off. The creature's name translates literally to hundred marsh or hundred languages, reflecting its comprehensive knowledge of all beings. In Chinese folk religion, Bai Ze is venerated as a protective oracle who can reveal hidden dangers and provide the knowledge needed to counter malevolent spirits. The legend of Bai Ze has influenced Chinese literature, art, and religious practice for over a thousand years, with its image appearing on protective talismans and temple murals throughout China
source: Chinese mythology; the Bai Ze is a chimeric beast that knows all spirits.

name: Baiame
description: Baiame is the supreme creator god and sky father in the mythology of several Aboriginal Australian peoples of southeastern Australia, including the Kamilaroi, Wiradjuri, and Eora nations. In the Dreamtime, Baiame descended from the sky world to create the land, plants, animals, and humans. He gave the people their laws, customs, and ceremonies before returning to the sky, where he remains watching over the world from his home in the Milky Way. Baiame established the rules of marriage, the totem system, and the proper relationships between people and land. His wives include Birrahgnooloo (associated with fertility and floods) and Cunnembeillee. Baiame is portrayed in rock art as an enormous figure with radiating headgear suggesting divine power. His son Daramulum acts as an intermediary between Baiame and humans
source: Aboriginal Australian mythology, southeastern oral traditions

name: Bajrak (Orang Bati)
description: Bajrak, also known as Orang Bati, is a fearsome flying demon from the folklore of Seram Island in the Maluku archipelago of eastern Indonesia. The creature's name Orang Bati translates to bat man in the local Malay dialect, describing its batlike humanoid form. According to local legends, the Bajrak is a nocturnal predator that emerges from the caves and dense forests of Seram's interior mountains to hunt at night. The creature is particularly feared because of its reported taste for human flesh, especially that of children. Bajrak legends are most common in the traditional communities around Mount Binaiya, Seram's highest peak, where locals tell stories of babies and small children being snatched from their homes during the night. The creature has been reported for generations, with accounts dating back to the period of Dutch colonial presence in the region, when European observers recorded local testimonies about the flying demon. In contemporary times, the Bajrak has attracted the attention of cryptozoologists who speculate that the legend might be based on sightings of large fruit bats or unknown flying creatures inhabiting the island's remote interior
source: Indonesian folklore, oral traditions across the archipelago

name: Bakh
description: Bakh spirits are forest-dwelling beings from the folklore of Sudan, particularly among the peoples of the Nuba Mountains and surrounding regions. These creatures are described as hairy wild men who inhabit the dense forests and remote mountain areas, existing at the boundary between the human world and the untamed wilderness. In Sudanese folk belief, Bakh are neither fully animal nor fully human but occupy a liminal space between the two. They are ambivalent spirits, capable of both helping and harming humans depending on how they are treated. Traditional Sudanese stories describe the Bakh as guardians of the forest who enforce proper behavior toward nature, punishing those who hunt excessively or damage the forest while guiding lost travelers who show respect for the wilderness. The Bakh tradition reflects the deep connection between Sudanese peoples and their natural environment, serving as a reminder that the forest has its own inhabitants and rules that must be respected. In some accounts, Bakh are the spirits of people who were so closely connected to the forest in life that they merged with it after death, becoming guardians of the wild places they once loved
source: Sudanese folklore — forest spirit documented in Sudanese oral tradition.

name: Bakru
description: Bakru, also called Backoo or Bacro, is a malevolent forest spirit from the folklore of Suriname and the surrounding Guiana region of South America, rooted in the Afro-Caribbean traditions brought by enslaved Africans and adapted in the context of the Surinamese rainforest. According to traditional belief, Bakru are created by evil sorcerers using dark magic derived from Winti, the Afro-Surinamese spiritual tradition. The sorcerer creates a wooden doll or statue in human form and, through a ritual involving the sacrifice of a child or the use of a deceased child's soul, animates it with a corrupted spirit. The resulting Bakru is bound to serve its creator, performing evil deeds and accumulating wealth for the sorcerer. However, the Bakru is perpetually hungry and must be fed regularly, often with blood or milk. If not properly controlled, the Bakru will turn against its creator, causing destruction and death. Belief in Bakru remains strong in Suriname and among the Surinamese diaspora, with the creature representing the dangers of black magic and the moral consequences of dealing with dark forces for personal gain
source: Surinamese Winti folklore — Bakru forest dwarfs.

name: Baktan
description: Baktan is a giant figure from the folklore of Senegal and the broader West African Sahel region, associated with the construction of the mysterious megalithic stone circles found in Senegambia. The creature is described as an enormous humanoid being of superhuman strength who could move stones that would be impossible for ordinary humans to lift. In Senegalese oral tradition, Baktan is one of the ancient giants who inhabited the world before the current human era, beings with extraordinary powers who shaped the landscape and built monumental structures whose origins are now lost to history. The megalithic stone circles of Senegambia, particularly those found in the region of Kaolack and along the Gambia River, consist of thousands of carved stone pillars arranged in circles, some weighing several tons each. Local traditions attribute these mysterious constructions to giants like Baktan, who could carry these massive stones on their heads or shoulders and arrange them in patterns that hold astronomical or spiritual significance. Baktan represents the connection between the present world and the time of origins, when beings of immense power walked the earth and created structures that continue to inspire wonder and speculation
source: Senegambian folklore — Baktan giant figure.

name: Bakunawa (The Moon-Eating Serpent)
description: The Bakunawa is a massive sea serpent or dragon in Visayan and Bicolano mythology believed to cause eclipses by attempting to swallow the moon. Originally a beautiful sea goddess transformed into a serpent as punishment for loving a mortal, the Bakunawa rises from the ocean depths to chase the moon across the sky. According to legend, the supreme god Bathala created seven moons to illuminate the night, but the Bakunawa, amazed by their beauty, swallowed six of them. To prevent the loss of the final moon, people make loud noises with pots, pans, and drums during eclipses to frighten the serpent into releasing the moon. The Bakunawa's movements served as a geomantic calendar system for ancient Filipinos and were part of babaylan (shaman) rituals. It is usually depicted with a characteristic looped tail and a single horn on the nose
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakunawa

name: Bakwa
description: Bakwa is the legendary Snake King of the Kalinago people of Dominica — a great diamond-crested serpent with magical powers that slithered out of the sea and took residence in a cave in the mountains. According to the ancient Kalinago legend retold by children of Atkinson School, Bakwa used his powers to grant wishes to those who approached him with respect. Maruka, a Kalinago farmer, was the first to discover Bakwa and receive his blessings. The legend is associated with L'Escalier Tete Chien (Staircase of the Snake), a natural rock formation resembling a staircase rising from the Atlantic Ocean on Dominica's southern coast in the Sineku area of the Carib Territory. According to Kalinago tradition, this formation is the pathway made by the enormous boa constrictor when it emerged from the ocean
source: Dominica Kalinago oral tradition; snip The Snake King of the Kalinago (Papillote Press)

name: Bakwas
description: Bakwas is a significant spirit being from the mythology of the Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) people of the Pacific Northwest Coast of British Columbia, Canada. In Kwakwaka'wakw cosmology, the Bakwas is a wild spirit of the forest, sometimes described as a wild woman of the woods or a dangerous forest being that inhabits the deep wilderness far from human settlements. These beings are part of the complex spiritual ecology of the Kwakwaka'wakw world, where the forest is inhabited by numerous supernatural beings that demand respect and proper protocol from those who enter their domains. The Bakwas is particularly associated with the winter ceremonial season, when the boundaries between the human and spirit worlds grow thin and supernatural beings may be encountered. In Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, the Bakwas is not inherently evil but is dangerous because it operates according to different rules than humans, and its intentions may be incomprehensible to human understanding. Encounters with the Bakwas can result in spiritual power for those who are properly prepared, or madness and death for those who approach without respect. The Bakwas is one of many supernatural beings that feature in the elaborate ceremonial dances and rituals of the Kwakwaka'wakw winter ceremonies, where initiates may be possessed by or transformed into these spirits as part of their spiritual training
source: Kwakwaka'wakw folklore — Bukwus wild man of the woods documented in Pacific Northwest oral tradition.

name: Bama Dat
description: Bama Dat is a type of ghost or restless spirit from Burmese folklore, part of the rich tradition of nat spirits and ghost beliefs that permeate the spiritual life of Myanmar. The term Bama Dat refers specifically to the spirit of a person who died unjustly, violently, or without proper funeral rites, leaving their soul trapped between the world of the living and the afterlife. In Burmese Buddhist cosmology, a proper death with appropriate ceremonies is essential for the soul's successful journey to its next existence. Those who die under unjust circumstances, such as murder victims, executed criminals, or those whose deaths were not properly mourned, may become Bama Dat, lingering in the human world to haunt the living until justice is served or proper rites are performed. This belief reflects the deep importance of karma and justice in Burmese Buddhist thought, where unresolved wrongs must be addressed before spiritual peace can be achieved. The Bama Dat is different from the official nat spirits recognized in the Burmese pantheon of thirty-seven nats, being instead a more personal and localized spirit, typically associated with specific locations where the death occurred
source: Myanmar mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Bannick
description: The Bannick is a spirit being from Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) tradition, a type of manitou that inhabits the waters and forests of the Great Lakes and Canadian Shield regions. In Anishinaabe cosmology, the world is filled with spiritual beings of various types and power levels, from the great Gitchi Manitou or Great Spirit to the lesser manitous that guard specific places and natural features. The Bannick belongs to this latter category, being a localized spirit associated with particular lakes, rivers, or forest areas. While the Mishipeshu or underwater panther is the most powerful water spirit in Ojibwe tradition, the Bannick is one of the many lesser spirits that form the complex spiritual ecology of the Anishinaabe world. These spirits are essential to the proper functioning of the natural world, each fulfilling specific roles in maintaining balance and order. In Ojibwe understanding, humans must maintain good relationships with all these spirits, not just the major ones, as each controls access to some aspect of the natural resources and spiritual power that humans need to survive and thrive In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.
source: Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) spiritual tradition; documented in Great Lakes ethnographic records.

name: Bannik-Moist
description: The Bannik-Moist is a specific variant of the Bannik, a spirit from Slavic folklore, particularly Russian tradition, who inhabits bathhouses and steam baths. In Russian folk belief, the banya or traditional steam bath is a sacred yet dangerous place, inhabited by its own powerful spirit that must be respected. The standard Bannik is a capricious and sometimes malevolent spirit who demands proper behavior in the bathhouse, but the Bannik-Moist variant is described as somewhat more social and communicative. While the regular Bannik is known to be dangerous, particularly after midnight when it bathes itself and will attack anyone who disturbs it, the Bannik-Moist is more likely to engage with humans in riddles and conversation. This variant is particularly associated with public bathhouses rather than private family baths, where multiple people from the community gather. In Russian folklore, the bathhouse is a liminal space where the boundaries between the human world and the spirit world are thin, making it a prime location for encounters with spirits, divination, and supernatural experiences. The Bannik-Moist represents the more social aspect of bathhouse spirituality, the spirit that governs the communal experience of the banya rather than the dangerous solitary bather
source: Russian folklore — Bannik bathhouse spirit variant.

name: Banyan Deer (Nigrodhamiga Jataka)
description: The Banyan Deer is a central figure in the Nigrodhamiga Jataka, one of the most famous Buddhist Jataka tales recounting the previous lives of the Buddha. In this story, the Bodhisattva (future Buddha) was born as a magnificent golden deer named King Banyan Deer, leader of a herd of 500 deer in the forests near Benares (Varanasi). The king of Benares was an avid hunter who frequently rode out to hunt deer, causing chaos and death throughout the forest. To prevent indiscriminate killing, the Banyan Deer — along with the leader of the opposing monkey deer herd — made a pact with the king: one deer would voluntarily be sacrificed each day as the king's meal, sparing the rest. One day, a pregnant doe from the monkey deer herd was destined to die. Her leader refused to take her place, so she appealed to King Banyan Deer. Moved with compassion, the Banyan Deer took her place, laying his head on the chopping block. The human king, witnessing this extraordinary act of self-sacrifice by a mere animal, was deeply moved and granted sanctuary to all deer, establishing a protected forest where no creature could be hunted
source: Nigrodhamiga Jataka (Jataka Tales, Pali Canon), Khuddaka Nikaya

name: Baron Samedi
description: The Barmanou is a cryptid hominid from the mountainous regions of northern Pakistan, particularly the Chitral District and the Karakoram range along the border with China. Known locally as the Barmanou or Bar-Manu, this creature is considered Pakistan's equivalent of the Himalayan Yeti or North American Bigfoot, occupying a similar ecological and folkloric niche in South Asian mountain traditions. The name derives from local Khowar language terms describing a wild man of the mountains, and the creature has been part of the oral traditions of the Kalash, Kho, and Burusho peoples for centuries. Unlike the purely mythical entities of the region, the Barmanou is described as a physical, flesh-and-blood creature that leaves footprints, vocalizations, and occasional sightings reported by shepherds and mountaineers in the high valleys of the Hindu Kush and Karakoram ranges
source: Haitian Vodou — Baron Samedi is the loa of the dead, documented in Haitian religious ethnography.

name: Barong (Lion Protector)
description: Barong is the king of the spirits and the leader of the hosts of good in Balinese mythology. He is a lion-like mythological creature and the eternal opponent of Rangda, the demon queen. The Barong represents good, protective forces, while Rangda embodies evil and chaos. In the famous Barong dance performance, which reenacts the eternal battle between good and evil, Barong protects the village from Rangda's dark magic. The term 'barong' is derived from 'bahruang,' meaning 'bear,' and the Barong is considered a guardian spirit of the forest. The most common form is Barong Ket, depicted as a lion with a red head, thick white fur, and gilded jewelry adorned with mirrors. Barong is also identified with Banas Pati Raja, the fourth 'brother' or spirit child that accompanies a Balinese person throughout life
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barong_(mythology)

name: Bata
description: In the animist spiritual traditions of the Udmurt people, a Finno-Ugric ethnic group indigenous to the Volga region of western Russia, the bat animal-spirit is a guardian being associated with the transition between day and night, the visible and invisible worlds. The Udmurt traditional religion, known as Udmurt Vos, is a complex system of animist beliefs centered around nature worship, ancestor veneration, and the veneration of countless spirits inhabiting the natural world. Within this cosmology, bats occupy a special place as creatures that belong neither fully to the day world of humans nor to the night world of spirits, making them powerful intermediaries between the mundane and supernatural realms. Unlike the negative associations bats carry in many European traditions, Udmurt culture often views these creatures as protectors that bring good fortune and spiritual insight to those who respect their domain
source: Philippine folklore, indigenous oral traditions

name: Batammariba Ancestor Spirits
description: In the folk beliefs of the Philippines, particularly among the Tagalog and Visayan peoples, Bata is a class of guardian spirit that watches over specific places, objects, families, or individuals. The term bata in Philippine languages primarily means child, but in the context of folk spirituality it refers to a protective spirit that appears in a variety of forms and is bound to a particular location or bloodline. These spirits belong to the broader category of diwata or anito, the nature and ancestor spirits that form the foundation of traditional Philippine animist religion, which has persisted for centuries beneath a surface layer of Catholicism introduced by Spanish colonization. Bata spirits are typically benevolent and protective, serving as invisible guardians who warn their charges of danger and ward off malevolent supernatural forces that might threaten their domain
source: West African oral tradition, Akan/Ashanti folklore

name: Batibat
description: In the religious tradition of the Batammariba people, an ethnic group inhabiting the Atakora Mountains of northwestern Togo and neighboring Benin in West Africa, ancestor spirits known as Kumpo or Tiyebe form the foundation of spiritual life and social organization. The Batammariba, also known as the Tamberma or Somba, are renowned for their distinctive architecture of fortified clay tower houses called Tata Somba, which are designed to serve both as physical dwellings and as symbolic representations of the cosmos and the ancestral world. In Batammariba cosmology, death is not an end but a transition to the ancestral realm where the spirits of the departed continue to participate actively in the lives of their descendants, guiding, protecting, and disciplining the living members of the family lineage. The ancestor spirits are considered the true owners of the land and the ultimate authorities on matters of tradition, morality, and justice within the community
source: Philippine folklore, indigenous oral traditions

name: Bauk
description: In Lithuanian folklore, Baubas is a domestic fear entity or bogeyman figure that inhabits the shadowy corners of rural farmhouses, used by parents for generations as a disciplinary tool to frighten children into obedient behavior. The name Baubas derives from the Lithuanian verb baubti meaning to roar or bellow, referring to the low threatening sounds the creature is said to make in the darkness. Unlike the more complex and individualized supernatural beings of Lithuanian mythology such as the deity Perkunas or the fate goddess Laima, Baubas is a simple but effective household terror that belongs to a category of folklore figures found across virtually every human culture. In Lithuanian tradition, Baubas is one of several similar entities including the more specific Aitvaras and Kaukas, but Baubas is distinguished by its generic formlessness and its specific association with childhood discipline and the fear of the dark
source: Serbian folklore — Bauk monster documented in Serbian oral tradition.

name: Baykok
description: In Serbian and broader South Slavic folklore, Bauk is a bogeyman or dark forest creature used by parents to frighten children into obedience, belonging to the widespread Indo-European family of disciplinary night terrors that includes the Lithuanian Baubas, the English Bogeyman, and the Romanian Bau-Bau. The name Bauk derives from the Serbian verb baukati or bauknuti meaning to roar or utter a frightening sound, directly referencing the creature's characteristic growling vocalizations. Within the rich tapestry of Serbian folk mythology which includes complex beings like the vampire, the werewolf, and the household protective spirit, Bauk occupies a simpler but enduring role as the embodied fear of the dark and the unknown, particularly used in rural communities of Serbia, Bosnia, Montenegro, and Macedonia where traditional farming life kept families closely connected to the untamed forests surrounding their villages
source: Ojibwe folklore — Baykok skeletal spirit documented in Ojibwe oral tradition.

name: Bayon Face Spirit (Lokeshvara)
description: The Bayon Face Spirit refers to the 216 massive stone faces carved on the towers of the Bayon Temple at Angkor Thom, the legendary capital built by King Jayavarman VII (1181-1218 CE). According to Khmer tradition, these faces represent the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara (Lokeshvara) — the embodiment of compassion in Mahayana Buddhism — gazing in all four directions to protect the Khmer Empire. Local folklore adds that the faces bear the features of King Jayavarman VII himself, who ordered his countenance carved so that his subjects would always feel his presence. A darker legend tells of the architect blinded after completing the temple so he could never duplicate it; when he touched the stone faces, his sight was miraculously restored. The faces are believed to watch over Angkor Thom eternally, their serene smiles reflecting the compassion of the bodhisattva and the power of the god-king. The Bayon's 54 towers with four faces each create one of the world's most extraordinary spiritual monuments
source: Khmer oral tradition, Angkor Thom local legends, Jayavarman VII inscriptions

name: Beaivi
description: Beaivi is the supreme sun deity of Sami mythology, venerated as a goddess of the sun, spring, fertility, and mental health. In the Arctic regions of Sapmi where winter darkness lasts months, she was the most important divine figure. She travels through the sky with her daughter Beaivi-nieida in an enclosure covered with reindeer bones and antlers, bringing spring and light. The Sami believed that madness and depression were caused by her absence during the dark winter months. On the winter solstice, white reindeer were sacrificed in her honor to ensure her return — their meat threaded on sticks bent into rings and tied with bright ribbons in the Festival of Beaivi. Butter was smeared on doorposts to strengthen her as she regained her height in the sky. At summer solstice, sun-rings of leaves were hung in trees. She makes plants grow so reindeer flourish and brings wealth and prosperity to humans
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Bear Guardian of Cree
description: The Bear Guardian of Cree tradition holds a central place in Cree spirituality as one of the most powerful animal beings, representing medicine power and the deep wisdom of the forest. In Nehiyaw cosmology, the bear is revered not merely as an animal but as a teacher, healer, and spiritual guide who shares its knowledge with those who approach it with humility and respect. The bear taught the Cree people about medicinal plants, the proper way to hunt, and the importance of dreaming as a pathway to spiritual understanding. Cree elders speak of the bear as a relative who walks in both the human world and the spirit world, carrying messages between them. The Bear Guardian is particularly associated with dream quests and vision fasts, where individuals seeking spiritual guidance may encounter the bear in visions that reveal their life path and purpose
source: Canada mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections
